title: How To Handle Misbehavior Outside Of Your Classroom -classroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to reader questions, Linsin addresses how to handle rule-breaking that occurs while the class is with the teacher but outside the room, such as walking to lunch or at an assembly. He rules out sending students to time-out on the spot or pulling them aside for a talking-to, and instead recommends a three-step approach: teach in advance that class rules apply everywhere, with the one difference being that consequences are delivered once the class returns to the room; stay actively observant while away from the classroom rather than getting distracted; and enforce consequences upon return, using a notebook for documentation during longer outings like assemblies. He notes initial warnings can still be given on the spot, with only subsequent consequences delayed. The consistent message — that rules apply everywhere and will always be enforced — is what he says eliminates the temptation to misbehave once outside the room.
points: Misbehavior outside the classroom (hallways, assemblies) should be handled with the same rules, just with consequences delayed until the class returns to the room.
Teach in advance, with modeled examples, that class rules apply everywhere the teacher is present.
Stay actively observant while away from the classroom rather than getting distracted by chatting with colleagues.
Use a notebook to document who misbehaved during longer outings like assemblies, to be addressed back in the room.
Initial warnings can still be given on the spot; only subsequent consequences are delayed until returning to class.
quotes: It’s a thorny issue, because you can’t very well send your students to time-out.
Because as soon as your students learn that they can misbehave away from the classroom without consequence, the floodgates will open.
The first step is to teach your students that class rules apply wherever you are and that they’ll be enforced just the same.
As soon as you leave your classroom, it’s important to stay in position to observe closely and make sure your students are behaving to your expectations.
If you’re going to be away from class for a period of time, like an assembly, then it’s smart to bring along a notebook for documentation.
Students tend to misbehave away from the classroom when they’re unsure whether the class rules still apply.
They’ll behave no different than when they’re in the classroom.
